claims.says: Advisor flags virtual machines with low usage to resize or shut down, and notes that some low use is by design.
Advisor lists managed disks not attached to a VM for review (preview).
Advisor recommends VM reservations from usage over a look-back period, estimated per subscription.
Advisor recommends a savings plan commitment from recent eligible usage.

references.notes: Reliability only. Each recommendation has a Resource Graph query under kql/ named by its ID. WARA runs these (ref:wara). Claim IDs are APRL's own public IDs.

claims.says: Create scaling plans per region (scaling plans, medium).
Create a validation host pool (host pools, medium).
Configure scheduled agent updates for host pools (host pools, medium).
Use a unique OU when deploying host pools with domain-joined session hosts (host pools, medium).
Protect stateful session hosts with Azure Site Recovery (host pools, medium).

references.title: Azure Resource Inventory (ARI)
references.license: MIT in the repo; the PowerShell Gallery listing says otherwise, so check before reuse

claims.says: Inventories a whole Azure environment into an Excel workbook and a diagram; it has no JSON output.
Its draw.io diagram functions (Modules/Public/PublicFunctions/Diagram/) make no Azure calls and draw from the Resource Graph rows they are given, with no AVD host pool placement.

references.title: Autoscale scaling plans and example scenarios in Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: Autoscale turns session hosts on and off on a schedule to optimize deployment cost; ramp-down is usually when VMs shut down to save cost.
Power management autoscaling powers hosts on and off; dynamic autoscaling also creates and deletes hosts, for pooled host pools with a session host configuration.
A host pool has at most one scaling plan, and autoscale must not be combined with Azure Automation or other scaling tools on the same host pool.
In a pooled host pool, autoscale keeps the minimum percentage of hosts on and turns on more only when used capacity passes the capacity threshold.
Hibernate is available for personal host pools.
Autoscale overwrites drain mode in pooled host pools, so updates use exclusion tags.

references.title: Troubleshoot connection quality in Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: Up to 150 ms shouldn't affect work without rendering or video, 150 to 200 ms is fine for text, over 200 ms might affect user experience.
Review Azure's network latency statistics every two to three months in case the best region changes.

references.title: Understand and estimate costs for Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: AVD costs come from Azure resource consumption and from licensing, and the owner of the deployment pays them, not the users.
Session host VM instances usually cost the most; autoscale, savings plans and reserved instances reduce compute cost.
Features carry their own costs, such as Insights log data, App Attach and profile storage, and custom image template storage.
The pricing calculator's AVD module estimates session hosts and feature storage only; egress to Microsoft 365 and other features need separate estimates.
After deployment, track AVD costs in Cost Management and with tags, and use Insights usage to optimize.

references.title: Azure Virtual Desktop Insights glossary

claims.says: Input delay bands: good under 150 ms, acceptable 150 to 500 ms, poor 500 ms to 2 s, bad over 2 s.
Time to connect splits into user route, stack connected, logon (profiles, Group Policy, shell start, FSLogix) and shell start to shell ready; no target time is given.
Insights lists the recommended performance counters and their intervals for session hosts.

references.title: Use cases for Azure Virtual Desktop Insights

claims.says: Latency should generally be below 100 ms for ideal interaction; a session becomes broadly low quality over 200 ms.
Each session host's user input delay should ideally stay below 100 ms.
Use session history and idle host counts over time to design a scaling plan, then repeat to validate it.

references.title: Licensing Azure Virtual Desktop
references.notes: Licensing isn't visible to a Reader-only run; the method takes it from the operator (gap:finops-scope).

claims.says: Every user needs an eligible license; Windows client session hosts take a qualifying Microsoft 365, Windows Enterprise or VDA per-user license, Windows Server hosts take RDS CALs with Software Assurance or RDS subscription licenses.
Per-user access pricing is only for external commercial purposes, charged per user who connects in the month, and isn't available for Windows Server.
Users who already hold eligible licenses are still charged in a subscription enrolled in per-user access pricing, so serve them from a separate subscription.

references.title: Prerequisites for Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: Round-trip time from the client's network to the host pool's Azure region should be under 150 ms; put session hosts in the region closest to users.

references.title: Azure Virtual Desktop REST API specification, stable 2025-10-10
references.notes: The property names Resource Graph returns under properties for each AVD resource type.

claims.says: A host pool has hostPoolType, loadBalancerType, maxSessionLimit, preferredAppGroupType, startVMOnConnect, validationEnvironment, agentUpdate and publicNetworkAccess, among others.
A session host has status, sessions, allowNewSession, lastHeartBeat, agentVersion, updateState and resourceId, the virtual machine it runs on.
An application group has applicationGroupType and hostPoolArmPath, which links it to its host pool.
A scaling plan lists the host pools it applies to in hostPoolReferences, with a schedule and a time zone.

references.title: Tag Azure Virtual Desktop resources to manage costs

claims.says: Start tagging with host pools, because their VMs are usually the main cost of an AVD deployment.
Tags report cost only for resources they are directly assigned to, and a new or changed tag shows in Cost Management only after the resource reports activity.
The cm-resource-parent tag, set to the host pool's resource ID, groups costs by host pool in Cost Management without filters.

references.title: Decide between a savings plan and a reservation (Microsoft Cost Management)

claims.says: Choose reservations for continuous, stable workloads with no expected change of instance family or region.
Choose a savings plan when workloads change size, family, service or region.
Right-size first, fix existing commitments next, and only then buy new ones; discounts reduce rates, not waste.

references.title: Tutorial, create and manage budgets (Microsoft Cost Management)

claims.says: A budget alerts on actual or forecast cost; resources aren't affected and consumption isn't stopped.
Cost data is typically available within 8 to 24 hours and budgets are evaluated against it every 24 hours.
A budget can call an action group only at subscription or resource group scope.
Budgets evaluate actual cost, not amortized cost.

references.title: Understand Cost Management data

claims.says: Cost and usage data typically appears within 8 to 24 hours for EA and MCA subscriptions, and can take up to 72 hours for pay-as-you-go.
Open-month data is an estimate; the billing period usually closes up to 72 hours after it ends.

references.title: Group and allocate costs using tag inheritance (Microsoft Cost Management)

claims.says: With tag inheritance on, subscription and resource group tags apply to child resources' usage records (not to the resources), for EA, MCA and MPA billing accounts.

references.title: FinOps Framework overview (Microsoft's guide to the FinOps Foundation framework)
references.notes: Microsoft's summary of the FinOps Foundation's framework, with Microsoft's extensions mapped back to it. The Foundation's own site has no immutable pin, so we cite this page and link the Foundation from the method. The framework judges an organization's FinOps practice; an estate assessment judges one workload, so only the workload-level capabilities are used (gap:finops-scope).

claims.says: Six principles, among them that FinOps data should be accessible, timely and accurate, and that teams use the cloud's variable cost model with continuous small adjustments.
Teams iterate through three phases, Inform (visibility, allocation, budgets, forecasts), Optimize (reduce waste) and Operate (KPIs and governance).

Capabilities are grouped in four domains, understand usage and cost, quantify business value, optimize usage and cost, and manage the FinOps practice; workload optimization, rate optimization, licensing, allocation, budgeting and unit economics are among them.
Judge maturity per capability against the team's own targets rather than one global Crawl-Walk-Run level, and reassess every three to six months.

references.title: FinOps toolkit overview (Microsoft, open source)
references.license: Microsoft Learn content (link only); the toolkit itself is open source
references.notes: Prior art for cost tooling. Its hubs, workbooks and optimization engine already report and recommend across an organization's cost data; the family doesn't rebuild them, and avd-current-state may cite their output as evidence when an operator runs them.

claims.says: The toolkit offers FinOps hubs for cost reporting, Power BI reports, cost optimization and governance workbooks, the Azure Optimization Engine, a PowerShell module and open data such as pricing units.

references.title: What is FOCUS? (FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification, Microsoft's guide)
references.notes: Prior art for the cost data format. The method doesn't define a cost data format of its own; where it reads cost by meter, it names FOCUS columns.

claims.says: FOCUS is a provider-neutral format for cost and usage data, and Cost Management exports it.
Each FOCUS row carries list, contracted, effective and billed cost, so savings from negotiated and commitment discounts can be quantified.

references.title: Troubleshoot issues using Performance Monitor (Windows Server)

claims.says: Processor time bands: up to 50% healthy, 50 to 80% worth watching, over 80% critical.
A processor queue of two or more per processor while CPU is high means looking for the processes using it.
Log counters over one or two working days, then look for patterns by day and hour rather than reacting to one reading.

references.title: What are Azure Reservations? (Microsoft Cost Management)

claims.says: A reservation is a one- or three-year billing discount applied hourly to matching usage; it doesn't change the resources, so buy for consistent base usage.
A VM reservation covers compute only, not Windows software, networking or storage; Azure Files has its own capacity reservations.
Reservations can be exchanged for the same type and refunded within a yearly limit.

Host pools, application groups, workspaces and scaling plans are in the Resources table, with virtual machines, storage accounts, virtual networks, route tables and private endpoints.
Policy assignments are in the PolicyResources table.

references.title: Azure Retail Prices REST API overview

references.title: What are savings plans? (Microsoft Cost Management)

claims.says: A savings plan commits a fixed hourly spend for one or three years; unused commitment in an hour expires.
The compute savings plan covers VM infrastructure across sizes and regions, not software, networking or storage.
Savings plans can't be canceled or refunded.

references.title: Session host virtual machine sizing guidelines

claims.says: The page's numbers are generic guidelines for initial performance estimates only.
Multi-session maximum users per vCPU: light 6, medium 4, heavy 2, power 1.
Keep multi-session VMs between 6 and 24 vCPUs; four cores is the lowest for a stable multi-session VM.
Plan at least 30 GB of profile storage per user.

references.title: Azure Virtual Desktop Start VM on Connect FAQ

claims.says: Start VM on Connect doesn't deallocate hosts; signing users out or shutting down from the Start menu doesn't either, so deallocation needs autoscale or automation.

references.title: Configure Start VM on Connect for Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: Start VM on Connect reduces cost by powering session hosts on only when a user connects; in pooled host pools it starts one host when none is on and more only when the first reaches its session limit.
Connecting to a deallocated host takes longer while it powers on.

references.title: Optimizing Windows configuration for VDI desktops

claims.says: Disk cleanup tasks should all be tested before they're used.
Removing or updating built-in Store apps can make sysprep fail; the guide links the support article.

references.title: Design review checklist for Cost Optimization (Azure Well-Architected Framework)
references.notes: Fourteen recommendations, CO:01 to CO:14. Claim IDs are the checklist's codes, used to place a cost finding in the pillar as RE:04 does for reliability. Only the codes the FinOps method uses are listed. The page footer showed 2023-11-15 while the page metadata said 2025-10-30; the pin uses the metadata.

claims.says: Keep a cost model of initial cost, run rate and ongoing cost, and a budget that covers it with a buffer.
Collect daily cost data, review spend against budget and cost model, and alert at thresholds and on anomalies.
Set spending guardrails, such as release gates, policies, resource limits and access controls, and prefer platform automation.
Get the best rates, reviewing region, tier, consumption against commitment pricing and license portability.
Understand the billing meters and align usage to their increments, validating major cost drivers with a proof of concept.
Regularly remove or optimize unneeded and underused components.
Optimize each environment's cost, including its operating hours; nonproduction should emulate production with deliberate tradeoffs.
Optimize scaling costs against the cost model and the limits of each scale unit.
Consolidate resources and increase density where the workload allows.

references.title: Design review checklist for Reliability (Well-Architected Framework)
references.notes: Each pillar's checklist numbers its items (RE, SE, CO, OE, PE). The source repo is private, so the pin is the page's own git_commit_id and updated_at.

claims.says: Define reliability and recovery targets and use them as the base of the health model.
Add redundancy at several levels, especially for critical flows.
Scale on actual or predicted usage with little manual intervention.
Measure and track health continuously with uptime and reliability indicators.

references.title: Complete an Azure Well-Architected Review assessment

claims.says: The Well-Architected Review is a self-assessment of about 60 questions across the pillars, with an Azure Virtual Desktop workload variant listed under specialized reviews.
It can add Azure Advisor recommendations for one subscription or resource group only.
Brownfield workloads should repeat it on a cadence (every four months is the example), tracked as milestones.

references.title: Well-Architected Reliability Assessment (WARA)
references.notes: The owner chose WARA as the rule engine for live reliability checks (2026-10-20). Details as checked on avd-second-brain's landing-zone KB page the same day.

claims.says: Start-WARACollector, with -AVD for AVD resource types, runs APRL's queries and writes JSON.
WARA covers the Reliability pillar only.
The analyzer writes an Excel action plan; the reporter writes PowerPoint and needs Windows with PowerPoint.

references.title: Windows Desktop Optimization Tool (WDOT)
references.notes: The family's image optimization reference. Pinned to release v1.1, the commit avd-landing-zone's image build runs with a reviewed profile (scripts/image/wdot/). main (ff2574c, 2026-05-20) adds only an event log change since. WDOT supersedes VDOT, which has no license.

claims.says: Optimizations come in categories (services, scheduled tasks, autologgers, default user settings, local policy, network, disk cleanup, Appx packages and more), each item set to apply or skip in a JSON profile.
Only items whose OptimizationState is Apply run; the templates are a starting profile to review, not a verdict on every estate.
The optimizations change system behavior and should be tested outside production first.
The repository's LICENSE file is MIT, while its README and EULA describe sample code terms (illustration only, as is), and a non-interactive run must accept the EULA.

observations.observed: Budgets only alert, so the landing zone wires its budget to an action group that runs a Lock runbook, and avd-swarm's spend guard enforces caps before a lab run opens instead of relying on the budget. For AVD a plain deallocate isn't enough either, because Start VM on Connect and the scaling plan start the hosts again at the next sign-in or ramp-up; Lock drains, sets the scaling plan exclusion tag and turns Start VM on Connect off. The budget-to-runbook path hasn't run against a real deployment yet.

The landing zone prices the compiled plan from retail prices before anything is deployed, with run hours from the power settings and an upper bound where the schedule rather than use decides (168 hours a week without a scheduled stop). Lab runs in the family don't start without that written estimate, a cap and teardown evidence, and avd-swarm's spend guard refuses a run whose estimate has an unpriced line or passes a cap. Retail prices are list prices, so the estimate is an upper bound for anyone with negotiated rates or commitments.
Latency measured from Cloud Shell says nothing about users, because Cloud Shell runs in an Azure datacenter. Measure round-trip time from the user's device, against endpoints verified to be regional.

A real preflight run priced session hosts and OS disks as unmatched because the API returned lookalike meters with the same SKU and meter name, a CloudServices product at the Windows rate beside Virtual Machines at the base rate, and a Premium Page Blob meter beside Premium SSD Managed Disks. Private Link and NAT Gateway are listed only under the Global region. A price is matched on product, SKU and meter, and a line that matches none or several is reported with what it saw rather than guessed.

The run recorder spec keeps each run's expected and actual cost as contract C17 (avd-run-cost/v1), appends a reading until it is unchanged for 72 hours, and reports pending rather than a guess until then. For scale, an earlier one-host sandbox demo cost 0.97 USD for about eight hours. How long the actual took to appear in a pay-as-you-go sandbox hasn't been measured yet (the spec's open question U5).

The landing zone deploys a power management scaling plan (depth-first ramp-down that stops hosts at zero sessions, without forcing sign-out) and Start VM on Connect on by default, and every resource group and resource carries workload and environment tags. No run has yet compared a month of running hours with the schedule, so the saving is Microsoft's claim, not our evidence. The landing zone doesn't set the cm-resource-parent tag.

The landing zone's minimum kit defaults to a 4-vCPU memory-optimized host, which is Microsoft's stated floor and below its 6 to 24 vCPU range, chosen for the smallest test cost. The reasoning that shared hosts run out of memory before CPU is our hypothesis; no measurement backs it yet.

Adopted as the landing zone's automatic sizing input, and its preflight warns above 6 sessions per vCPU. No real users have been measured against it, so the numbers are still Microsoft's prior, not our evidence.
The landing zone's image build keeps WDOT's Appx package removal off for this reason; no sysprep failure has been seen with it off. Not yet tested with it on.

WDOT's DiskCleanup category deletes every log, trace and event log file on the system drive, including an image build's own evidence before the image test reads it. The landing zone keeps that category off and cleans narrowly instead.

What runs inside the guest isn't visible from the control plane, but the landing zone's image build tags each gallery image version with the WDOT release, commit and profile hash it ran, so a Reader can see which pin and profile an image claims. Images built any other way carry no such record.
